prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of flat bands in twisted bilayer graphene at a magic angle and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B017 alone, with MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero and Bistritzer. It remains the shortlist case in which a quantitative prediction (the 2011 continuum model with a magic angle where the bandwidth collapses) was followed by an experiment that found what the model made plausible: gate-tunable correlated insulators and superconductivity near that angle. The consequence is a new field, moire quantum matter, now carried by many laboratories and several material platforms. The three names follow the structure of the discovery without an arbitrary cut. I have not hidden from myself that six colleagues prefer B001, and I have tried to test my position against their arguments and not against their count. Their case is real and I would not call a B001 prize wrong. But nothing in round 1 changed my reading of the science: the maturity objection is about the pairing mechanism, and the discovery being rewarded is the flat-band platform and its correlated states, not a theory of pairing.
statement.case_against: The reservations I take most seriously are attribution and timing. Yuan Cao, first author of the decisive 2018 papers, is outside the three-person limit, as are Dean, Young, Yacoby, Efetov and others who built the wider program, and an unusually fast, crowded field invites the charge of picking a winner too early. If the committee wanted a condensed-matter prize that is secure against that charge, waiting a few years would be defensible, and Mehlig and Olsson are right that the case may look stronger then. I also accept that B001 is the better-defined, more independently confirmed achievement today, with a two-name credit that nobody on the committee disputes. My own case is therefore weaker on attribution and maturity than B001 and stronger on a clean prediction-to-experiment line and on how much new physics it opened.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B017 third and calls it a stronger case in a few years if the mechanism question is clearer, and treats Cao's absence from the credit as an attribution problem.
responses.response: I agree on Cao and I still think the committee should say openly, in its public account and not only in a footnote, that the three-person limit forces credit to the group through its leader and that the first author is part of that group. Where I disagree is on waiting for the mechanism. The mechanism of superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene may take a long time to settle, as with the cuprates, and a prize that waits for it is a prize for a different discovery than the one on the table. What would move me is not mechanism but a decision by the committee that attribution within the Jarillo-Herrero group cannot be stated honestly in three names; if colleagues who know the experimental history show that, I would accept deferral.

responses.point: Olsson calls B017 the clear first alternative and says giving the prize now would fix the allocation before the experimental history has settled.
responses.response: I take that seriously because she works in oxide interfaces and knows how fast a crowded device field can reassign credit. My answer is that the allocation here is not really unsettled at the level of the prize: the prediction is Bistritzer and MacDonald, and the first demonstration of correlated and superconducting states at the magic angle is the Jarillo-Herrero group, with Dean, Young and others following after and supporting the finding. That later work is evidence that the result held, not a competing claim to the first observation. I accept that the fractional Chern and other moire discoveries need separate recognition, if at all, and my narrow citation is meant to leave room for them.

responses.point: Kroll holds B001 as a distinct instrument-driven invention, thinks the 1989, 2005 and 2012 precedents are a presentational point, and says B017 is not more secure than B001.
responses.response: I accept the second half and in round 1 I said so about attribution. B001 is more secure today: independent confirmation at several national laboratories and two names that map onto concept and record performance. On the precedents I cannot judge from my own field, so I defer to him, Lindroth and Mehlig, who say the lattice clock is a separate invention from the comb and from ion control, and who treat the overlap as a matter for the citation. Given that, I do not regard the precedents as a bar to B001 and would say so if a B001 configuration is the committee's choice. My disagreement is that security of attribution is one criterion, and the size of the new physics opened is another, where I weigh B017 higher.

responses.point: Pearce asks whether B027 is complementary to a clocks prize or only a lower-ranked option, and prefers a clocks-only prize as cleaner.
responses.response: I see B027 as a lower-ranked option, not a complement. My objection from round 1 stands: one name for a collaboration-scale instrument, with proposers, builders and analysts left out, and source identifications at moderate significance. Adding it to B001 would also make the prize look like two unrelated halves chosen to widen support. If the committee goes with B001, I agree with him that clocks alone is the cleaner form, and I note that his own statement offers to drop B027 for exactly that reason.

responses.point: Eriksson agrees that Cao and the wider moire community are the weak point, and that the group-leader convention is defensible but open to criticism.
responses.response: We agree on the shape of the case and on its weakness, and I do not think we should overstate it. I would add one thing to his caution: the group-leader convention is not new to the prize, and the point is to be explicit about it and not apologetic. His restraint about extending the citation to fractional Chern insulators and other moire results is also mine.

uncertainties: Whether the committee judges eight years and an open pairing mechanism to be early; I think it is a normal horizon, but five colleagues disagree and I cannot show that they are wrong.
Whether experimental credit can be stated honestly as the Jarillo-Herrero group through its leader when the first author is excluded by the three-person cap.
Whether lattice clocks are distinct enough from the 2005 and 2012 prizes; I cannot judge this from outside atomic physics and defer to the atomic-physics members, whose view is that they are.
Whether the committee prefers the maturity and cleaner two-name credit of B001 this year over the larger new-physics case of B017; this is a weighing of criteria, not a factual question.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with any credited person on the shortlist is apparent from my profile. My documented ties (David Gross as PhD supervisor, Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet, the Uppsala theory group) involve none of them. I do not work in condensed matter or atomic physics. On Kroll's Hall-laboratory link to B001 and the chair's astroparticle proximity to B027, I have no basis to ask for recusal and would leave that judgment to the chair.
